assign.now: measuring — the repo census and three timed worktree adds

log.msg: THE NUMBER THAT CHANGES THE ANSWER. The working tree is 826 MB, but only 254 MB of it is TRACKED, and `git worktree add` copies tracked files only. public/notes/inbox (407 MB) and public/framework/ai/**/shots/ (143 MB) are both gitignored, so no worktree ever sees them. Measured 2026-09-22 14:58-15:05, michael/dev at 3e9536d4, working tree dirty by 10 files.

Census, from `git ls-tree -r -l HEAD`: 8,187 tracked files / 254.4 MB. The two counts that must agree DO agree — `git ls-files | wc -l` is 8,187 and the directory table sums to 8,187. Top dirs by bytes: public/framework/ai 150.0 MB / 2,939 files; public/websites/site 38.2 MB / 283; public/imagine/design 6.9 MB / 631; public/framework/ext 5.8 MB / 1,201; public/layouts/browse 5.4 MB / 263; public/framework/styles 4.0 MB / 334; public/framework/core 2.9 MB / 801; public/imagine/paging 2.8 MB / 111; public/blog/ai 2.4 MB / 45; public/notes/doodles 2.0 MB / 28.

Generated bulk vs hand-written source: images are 206 MB of the 254 MB tracked (117.5 MB of .png across 1,115 files, 88.2 MB of .jpg across 1,929). Hand-written source — every .js, .css, .md, .mjs outside the ai log and notes — is 17.1 MB across 3,177 files. Put plainly: 81% of what a worktree copies is screenshots, and 7% is the code anyone is editing.

TIMED, on this machine, today. Full worktree (`git worktree add --detach`): 3.1 s, 274 MB on disk, 8,187 files, plus 1.1 MB of bookkeeping in .git/worktrees/. The 235 MB object store is NOT duplicated — the worktree's .git is a one-line text file pointing back at the main .git. Sparse limited to public/framework/ai + Server + root files: 1.6 s, 159 MB, 3,002 files. Sparse limited to the CODE (framework/core, ext, ui, styles, web, Server, .claude): 0.8 s, 21 MB, 2,564 files.

Sparse is per-worktree and cannot leak. The pattern file lands at .git/worktrees/<name>/info/sparse-checkout; the main checkout answered `fatal: this worktree is not sparse` and still had all 8,187 files on disk after both sparse worktrees existed.

The prior study's estimate of about 805 MB per worktree (7.25 GB at nine) is high by 3x against today's measurement of 274 MB. Most likely it counted the working tree (826 MB) rather than the tracked files a checkout actually writes, or assumed a copied node_modules. Recording the disagreement rather than quietly replacing the number.

assign.now: probing Claude Code's own worktree isolation, then proving the existing scripts

log.msg: CLAUDE CODE'S BUILT-IN --worktree IS STILL UNUSABLE HERE, and now I can name the commit. CLI 2.1.260 has `-w, --worktree [name]`. It puts the worktree INSIDE the repo at .claude/worktrees/<name>, on a new branch worktree-<name>, marks it locked, and adds `**/.claude/worktrees/` to .git/info/exclude so git status stays quiet. But it cuts from b55a7cae — the last merge commit on main — not from the checked-out michael/dev HEAD. Measured: 815 files on disk instead of 8,187; `git diff --stat 3e9536d4 b55a7cae` is 7,887 files changed, 799,876 deletions. An agent in it sees a repo with no ai/ log, no imagine/, no layouts/, no websites/. Same verdict as 2026-09-18, re-proven today with the number.

WHERE A WORKTREE MUST NOT GO, from reading the server rather than guessing. Server/watch.js is ONE recursive fs.watch handle on public/ and nothing else, so a worktree at .claude/worktrees/ or a sibling of the repo is invisible to live reload. A worktree UNDER public/ is a different story: Server/plugins/Directory.js build_dir() walks public/ recursively and skips only `.git` and `node_modules`, so every file of the worktree lands in directory.json (already 2.6 MB) and the ai dashboard, which enumerates task dirs from that file, would show a duplicate of every task. Worse, the checkout itself writes 8,187 files in about 3 seconds — exactly the burst watch.js warns can overflow Windows' ReadDirectoryChangesW buffer and DROP events — while each directory.json rebuild is a ~110 ms blocking walk of a tree that just doubled.

WHY Server/worktree-up.mjs HAD NEVER BEEN PROVEN ON THIS REPO — it was not the script. The safe-rollout session (2026-09-21, log line 11:38) had its own Bash/PowerShell tools refuse every command that executes code or mutates git: `node --check`, `node -e`, even read-only `node Server/hold.mjs`, and `git worktree add`. It shipped the scripts unable to run them once.

PROVEN TODAY, first try: `node Server/worktree-up.mjs wtd-proof` took 3.8 s end to end — worktree at C:/Code/lew42/worktrees/wtd-proof, node_modules junctioned from the main checkout, a server booted on a free port (50435) answering HTTP 200. Real pages served: / and /framework/ 200 (2,870 bytes), /app.js 200 (7,495 bytes). It booted happily alongside the five dev servers already on this machine — no fixed-port collision — and Whisper skipped itself, because Server/plugins/Whisper.js already treats any PORT other than 80 as not owner-facing (so NO_WHISPER=1 is belt-and-braces, not required).

DEFECT FOUND IN Server/worktree-down.mjs — teardown can never succeed, so every worktree leaks. worktree-up.mjs writes the server's stdout to `.worktree-server.log` INSIDE the worktree; worktree-down.mjs then refuses to remove the worktree because `git status --porcelain` is non-empty — showing only that same log file. It stops, deletes the registry entry anyway, and leaves 278 MB and a branch on disk with nothing tracking them. That is precisely the SSD bloat the owner is worried about, caused by the cleanup path never firing. One-line fix, for whoever owns Server/: at creation, append `/.worktree-server.log` to `.git/worktrees/<name>/info/exclude` (git reads $GIT_DIR/info/exclude, and for a linked worktree $GIT_DIR is that per-worktree directory — the same place `sparse-checkout` lands, verified today). Not applied: this brief is paper-only and forbids edits under Server/.

MEMORY COST OF ONE MORE DEV SERVER, from Win32_Process: my fresh worktree server was a 57 MB supervisor plus a 68 MB Server/run.js child, about 125 MB. The five main-tree run.js processes already running, warm and having built their own directory.json, sit at 212-243 MB each (health.mjs is another 206 MB). So budget ~125 MB for a new worktree server and ~230 MB once it is warm; three parallel teams cost roughly 0.7 GB of RAM, not disk.

CLEANUP PROVEN. All four experimental worktrees (wt-full, wt-sparse, wt-code outside the repo, wtdprobe inside .claude/) plus the wtd-proof one were removed, `git worktree prune` run, and both branches I created (worktree-wtdprobe, worktree/wtd-proof) deleted. `git worktree list` is back to the single main entry and the main checkout still has all 8,187 files. The only trace left is an empty, git-excluded .claude/worktrees/ directory that Claude Code recreates on demand.

WHAT A RESTRUCTURE WOULD SAVE, counted not guessed. Pulling the 1,084 screenshots under public/framework/ai/ (120.3 MB) out of the tracked tree alone takes a full worktree from 254 MB to 134 MB — 47% off with one rule, and the .gitignore already has its sibling (public/framework/ai/**/shots/). Adding the website corpus public/websites/site/ (38.2 MB, 283 files) takes it to 96 MB. Every remaining tracked image anywhere (design references 6.7, layout shots 9.8, blog 3.3, the rest 29.5) would take it to 47 MB across 5,093 files.

INCIDENT, MINE, CAUSED AND REPAIRED IN ABOUT 90 SECONDS — and it is the second and worse defect in Server/worktree-up.mjs. That script junctions node_modules from the main checkout into the worktree. When I then ran `git worktree remove`, the removal walked THROUGH the junction and emptied the MAIN checkout's real node_modules: 68 packages gone, express/chokidar/ws with them. The 2026-09-19 worktree-study log warned about exactly this ('UNSAFE -- worktree removal deleted the main tree's real copy') and the script still shipped the junction, with a comment arguing for it. I reproduced it independently today.

WHAT THE DAMAGE ACTUALLY WAS, and what it was not. The five dev servers running off this tree already had their modules loaded in memory, so nothing went down: port 80 answered 200 throughout, and all five Server/run.js PIDs (30992, 9572, 28144, 36532, 38172) are the same before and after. The real exposure was the NEXT restart -- a sibling minion saving any file under Server/ restarts every supervised server, and it would have died on `Cannot find package 'express'`. Repaired with `npm install` from the package-lock.json already in the tree: 1.0 s, 68 packages back, express/chokidar/ws present, `git diff package-lock.json` empty. No dependency added, no version moved.

decision.about: How a worktree gets its node_modules, given that the junction in Server/worktree-up.mjs destroys the main tree's copy on removal

options.say: keep the junction (fs.symlinkSync ... 'junction') the script uses today
options.why: no network, no duplicated files, instant -- but PROVEN TWICE now (2026-09-19 and again today) to let `git worktree remove` delete the main checkout's real node_modules

options.say: run `npm install` inside the new worktree
options.why: measured at 1.0 s today and 871 ms in the prior study, for 3 direct dependencies and 68 packages; the worktree owns its own copy, so removal can only ever delete its own

options.say: copy the main tree's node_modules into the worktree
options.why: no network either, but thousands of files per worktree and it goes stale the moment package.json moves

decision.why: A one-second install is not worth a class of bug that silently breaks every dev server on the machine at its next restart. The cost the junction was avoiding (time, disk) is a rounding error next to 68 packages vanishing from under five running servers.

log.msg: So Server/worktree-up.mjs and worktree-down.mjs each carry one defect that must be fixed before anyone is told to use them: up.mjs must `npm install` instead of junctioning node_modules, and it must keep its `.worktree-server.log` out of the worktree (or exclude it via .git/worktrees/<name>/info/exclude) so down.mjs can actually remove what it made. Both are small; neither is applied here, because this brief is paper-only and forbids edits under Server/. They belong to whoever owns Server/ next.

decision.about: How three parallel teams should pay for their worktrees on this SSD

options.why: 274 MB each, 822 MB for three, 3.1 s to create; nothing 404s and Server/worktree-up.mjs already does it

options.say: sparse worktrees materialising only the task's directories
options.why: 21 MB and 0.8 s for a code task, 63 MB for three teams -- but the dev server then serves a partial site and every page outside the cone 404s, so you cannot click around it

options.say: move the generated bulk out of the tracked tree first
options.why: pulling the 1,084 screenshots under public/framework/ai/ takes a full worktree from 254 MB to 134 MB, 402 MB for three teams -- 47% off in one rule

decision.why: 822 MB against 771 GB free is one tenth of one percent. The worry was real but the number was not: the 826 MB everyone was reacting to is mostly the gitignored notes inbox, which a worktree never copies. Sparse wins the moment you want MANY worktrees at once -- the nine-masterminds-on-one-target idea -- and is worth having ready for that. Restructure is worth doing anyway, on its own merits, because it halves every clone, fetch and checkout forever; it is just not the thing standing between us and worktrees.

decision.about: Where a worktree lives on disk

options.why: outside the repo entirely, so the dev server's one recursive fs.watch handle on public/ can never see it; already what Server/worktree-up.mjs does

options.say: .claude/worktrees/<name>/, inside the repo -- Claude Code's own default
options.why: inside the repo but outside public/, so it also dodges the watcher and the directory builder; git-excluded automatically -- but the CLI cuts it from the wrong commit, which is the disqualifier, not the location
nothing recommends it: Directory.js walks public/ recursively skipping only .git and node_modules, so every worktree file lands in directory.json and the ai dashboard shows a duplicate of every task

decision.why: It is the only location that is invisible to both the watcher and the directory builder without depending on a git exclude, and it is where the existing script already puts them.

assign.outcome:
**A second copy of this repo costs 274 MB, not 826 MB — so give every parallel team a full worktree and stop worrying about the SSD.** Two thirds of what you see on disk is gitignored and a worktree never copies it. Three teams working at once cost about 0.8 GB out of the 771 GB free on this drive.

The whole answer is one page: [Worktrees without the bloat](/framework/ai/2026-09-22/worktree-design/) — the recommendation, the five-line rule for who gets a worktree, the measured numbers, and the three ways to pay for it, with where a worktree goes, the per-worktree dev server, and how two rival teams merge one click down.

![the page](/framework/ai/2026-09-22/worktree-design/shots/page.png)

**Two defects found in the scripts that already exist, and one of them bit me while I was proving them.** `Server/worktree-up.mjs` junctions node_modules into the new worktree, and removing that worktree follows the junction and empties the MAIN checkout's real node_modules — 68 packages, express among them. The running servers survived because they already had their modules in memory; the next restart would not have. Repaired in one second with `npm install`, package-lock.json untouched. And `Server/worktree-down.mjs` can never remove what it made — it refuses on the log file worktree-up.mjs itself wrote inside the worktree, so every worktree leaks 278 MB and a branch. Both fixes are one line; neither is applied, because this brief is paper-only and may not edit `Server/`.

**Claude Code's own `--worktree` is still unusable here, and now I can name why.** CLI 2.1.260 puts it at `.claude/worktrees/<name>` and cuts it from `b55a7cae` — the last merge commit on `main` — not from your checked-out `michael/dev`. That is 815 files against 8,187, and 799,876 deletions.

**Deliberately left:** the two `Server/` fixes, for whoever owns that tree next (both named exactly, with the one-line change, in the log). The usage snapshot refresh, because my fence did not name those shared files. And nothing was pruned — the restructure numbers are a proposal to look at, not a change.
